I'll go with **American Express** — there's a lot that's genuinely interesting about how they're built differently from the rest of the industry.

**The core structural difference:** Visa and Mastercard are just networks — they don't lend money or issue cards; banks do that, and the networks collect small fees for routing transactions. Amex is a "closed loop" system: it operates the network, issues most of its own cards, and lends to its own customers. This means it owns the entire relationship and sees all the data, but it also means it carries the credit risk.

**The business model consequence:** Because Amex isn't competing to be in every wallet, it charges merchants higher fees (historically around 2.5-3.5% vs. roughly 2% for Visa/Mastercard). It justifies this by delivering affluent customers who spend more. That's why for decades plenty of restaurants and small retailers simply didn't take it — the "do you take Amex?" question was a real thing. Amex has spent the last decade aggressively closing that gap with its OptBlue program for small merchants, and US acceptance is now roughly on par with the other networks, though international acceptance still lags noticeably.

**Revenue mix:** This is the part most people find surprising. Amex makes the majority of its money from *discount fees* (merchant fees) and annual card fees — not from interest on revolving balances. Most big issuers depend heavily on people carrying debt. Amex's customers skew toward paying in full, which historically meant lower credit losses during recessions. Charge cards (as opposed to credit cards) were the original product: no preset limit, but the balance is due in full each month.

## Why Costco is interesting

**The core trick:** Costco barely makes money selling things. Its gross margins on merchandise hover around 11% — a fraction of typical retailers — and it caps markups at 14% on branded goods, 15% on Kirkland Signature. Most of its operating profit comes from **membership fees**, which are nearly pure margin. In recent years, membership revenue has been roughly comparable to total net income.

So Costco is better understood as a **subscription business that happens to own warehouses**, where the merchandise is the perk you get for subscribing.

**What makes it durable:**
- **Membership renewal rates** run around 90% in the U.S. and Canada — stickiness that most subscription businesses would envy.
- **SKU discipline.** A typical Costco warehouse carries roughly 4,000 items versus 30,000+ at a supermarket. Fewer SKUs means massive volume per item, which means enormous supplier leverage and faster inventory turns.
- **Negative working capital dynamics.** Costco often sells inventory before paying suppliers for it, effectively financing growth with supplier money.
- **Kirkland Signature** is one of the great private-label stories — a store brand that customers actively seek out rather than settle for, now generating tens of billions annually.

**The employee angle:** Costco pays well above retail norms and has unusually low turnover. This isn't charity — low turnover reduces training costs and keeps experienced staff who move pallets efficiently. It's a case study in whether "treat workers well" and "maximize profit" can genuinely align.

**Risks worth watching:** The model depends on continued membership growth, which eventually bumps into market saturation in mature geographies. International expansion (especially China) carries execution risk. And e-commerce has been a structural weakness — the treasure-hunt, buy-in-bulk experience doesn't translate neatly to a website, though they've improved.
